title: Vesak
hook: the May full moon: in Theravada lands, birth, awakening and passing remembered on one day

segments.voice: Yesterday, your morning: bow, homage, breath, metta, dedication, and sadhu three times. Your line was a morning, yours. Did you get ten minutes before the phone? Day one hundred forty-five, and a new week: the holy days.

A birthday, a graduation and a funeral, all on the same day. Every year. With lanterns. That's roughly what the full moon of May holds across Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos, and in Buddhist communities worldwide. Streets fill with lights. Temples fill up. People dressed in white carry flowers and candles. It's a great holy day in these countries, and it holds three moments of one life at once. Today's word is its name.
screen: `A BIRTHDAY, A GRADUATION, A FUNERAL.` → `ALL ON ONE FULL MOON.` → `THREE MOMENTS OF ONE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Vesak. The name comes from Vesakha, the month in the old Indian calendar that usually falls in April or May. In Theravada tradition, three events in the Buddha's life are remembered on the full moon of that month. His birth, in the garden at Lumbini. His awakening, under the tree at Bodh Gaya. And his passing into final nibbana, at Kusinara, eighty years later. Born, awake, gone: the whole life held in one night. The awakening is remembered in the Dhammapada with a verse tradition places on the Buddha's lips that night, addressed to craving as the builder of the house of the self. In Max Muller's translation: "But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again." And his passing is remembered with his last words, in the long discourse on the final nibbana. In T. W. Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" The same night holds a baby's first breath and an old man's last. Tradition doesn't treat that as an accident of the calendar. It reads like the teaching itself: things arise, things pass, and in between, a person can wake up. In 1950 a gathering of Buddhists from many countries, the World Fellowship of Buddhists, agreed to keep Vesak together, and in 1999 the United Nations recognized it too. Other Buddhist traditions keep these events on separate days; you'll meet one of them tomorrow. And because it follows the moon, the date moves: some years it falls in June. The lamp people light that night isn't for one moment. It's for the whole life.
screen: `VESAKHA: THE APRIL-MAY MOON.` · `BORN AT LUMBINI.` · `AWAKE AT BODH GAYA.` · `GONE AT KUSINARA.` · then, large: `BORN, AWAKE, GONE.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Hold three moments of one life in your mind, slowly. A baby's first breath, in a garden. A man under a tree at dawn, seeing clearly. An old man lying between two trees, saying: keep going, with care. Now feel your own breath: it too began once, and it will end once. And right now, in between, it's here. Rest in this one. The bell holds the time.
Vesak. The full moon of Vesakha, when Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on one day.
Your line: born, awake, gone. Tonight, light a lamp or a candle, for the whole of a life, and look up when this year's Vesak moon falls. Day one hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: On Vesak, Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing: many dress in white, visit temples, keep extra precepts, give food and light lanterns and lamps.

trapdoor: what you thought: Vesak is the Buddha's birthday.
what it means: in Theravada, birth, awakening and final passing, all remembered on one full moon.
what a scholar hears: the three-in-one Vesak was affirmed by the World Fellowship of Buddhists in 1950, and the UN recognized the Day of Vesak in 1999.
